notes: substrate-as-vocabulary. rung 1-8 per category, matching the Yegge/ai-levels.org N-ladders-x-8-rungs shape (see README's 'Where this ladder comes from'). Every non-empty rung's definition is synthesized directly from its evidence_row_ids' practice text -- no rung content was invented past what the corpus actually supports. Rungs with row_count 0 are left with definition: null and status: no_corpus_evidence rather than filled from the Yegge/ai-levels.org template text, per the project's own rejection of hand-tagging and fabricated rung content. Revised 2026-08-29 across four targeted low-rung sourcing passes (corpus batches 'm' through 'p' -- Claude Code's, Cursor's, and GitHub Copilot's own docs, Steve Yegge's primary essay, and every.to's 'AI & I' podcast, sourced via YouTube auto-captions after every.to's own transcript pages proved to be a systematic paywall dead end). 46 of 48 cells are now grounded. parallelization rung 5 -- the hole two prior passes searched and came up empty on -- landed on the third try, from a podcast source rather than vendor docs: practitioners describing an opportunistic, no-governing-rule burst of concurrent sessions, distinct from rung 6's deliberate numeric-scaling discipline. One genuine hole remains: prompting_structure rungs 7-8, which looks structural rather than a sourcing gap -- a meta/no-rung corpus row (m4, corroborated by a second independent source) argues that at the frontier 'prompting' stops being a distinct skill and generalizes into harness engineering, with that frontier practice already living in this corpus under trust_qa/context_mgmt/agent_invocation instead. A tool meant to meet a user wherever they actually are now has real ground under every rung but two.

rungs.definition: No deliberate prompt is authored at all: the whole interaction is accepting or rejecting inline 'ghost text' completions keystroke by keystroke while typing, rather than issuing any instruction -- completions-based coding as the pre-prompting floor.

First deliberate prompting, still fully unstructured: issue an instruction in chat, get a result, feed it back and ask for more, in a continuous ad hoc loop with no reuse across turns or sessions -- 'vibe coding' as a prompting style rather than a trust question.

Two adjacent practices at this altitude: (1) using the agent for narrow scaffolding and setup friction rather than full design-through-implementation work, deliberately bounding trust after direct experience with subtly-wrong autonomous output that had to be thrown away; (2) prompting with deliberate specificity -- scoping a task to a named file and scenario, pointing at the specific source that answers a question, referencing existing codebase patterns to model new work on -- specificity replacing ad hoc back-and-forth, but still one-shot asks rather than a structured plan-first workflow.

Prompts start carrying content beyond prose: reference files directly instead of describing where code lives, paste images to specify a visual target, pipe data straight into the prompt, and hand over documentation URLs rather than re-explaining an API from memory -- a richer input modality, still short of deliberate plan-first discipline.

Prompts deliberately and at the right specificity: starts sessions in explicit plan-first mode before allowing any edits, writes instructions at the 'right altitude' (concrete enough to steer, flexible enough to leave room for judgement), and treats the prompting medium itself (e.g. voice dictation) as a lever on prompt quality.

Prompting becomes reusable infrastructure: prompts for repeated workflows are checked into git as versioned commands/files instead of retyped, the agent is given standing orders to interview and disambiguate before starting from an underspecified brief, and a working-but-mediocre first pass is explicitly discarded and reimplemented rather than patched.

The floor of the trust ladder, defined by its own boundary case: accept and use agent output in a continuous ask-feed-back-ask-again loop without inspecting the result at all -- what got named 'vibe coding' when chat-based coding first got a name.

Watches the diff stream in as the agent generates it and interrupts (stop/redirect) the moment it looks wrong, rather than letting a run finish before looking at anything -- reactive, in-the-moment correction, not yet a deliberate read-through of finished work.

First deliberate, full read-through of the diff before it goes anywhere else -- the same standard applied to hand-written code -- but still a single unaided human pass with no tooling or testing backing it up, sized to what's actually reviewable (breaking a change into smaller pieces if it's too large to read comfortably in one sitting).

The core trust boundary itself becomes a checkable line rather than a vibe: whether agent output is looked at at all (vibe coding: never look, forget it exists) versus given detailed review (agentic programming) -- and whether the codebase's own tooling (strong typing, compiler, LSP diagnostics) gives the agent a fast correctness feedback loop independent of human review.

Accountability and understanding stay explicitly human even as trust grows: an agent is never treated as the Directly Responsible Individual no matter how much of the work it does, and the practitioner deliberately builds real understanding of the architecture and dependencies being relied on rather than accepting a working-but-opaque change.

Verification becomes systematic and multi-channel: front-loaded alignment gates (spec, architecture, design) replace one large end-of-work review, automated grading rubrics and human testing run alongside each other, real end-to-end interface checks supplement unit tests, and review work increasingly moves to the agent itself or to process (golden-principle scans, sandboxing) instead of a human reading every line.

Review moves upstream and becomes structurally enforced: specs and plans get reviewed instead of diffs, architecture is enforced as compiler/linter-checked invariants rather than prescribed by hand, a second independent agent (sometimes deliberately from a different model family) adversarially reviews the first agent's plan or output before it ships, and policy is enforced by deterministic hooks rather than trusted to agent judgment.

Verification is engineered as a first-class system in its own right: agents verify their own work end-to-end against the real interface (browser automation as the single highest-leverage practice), multiple decorrelated review lenses are stacked and trusted as a combination over any one perfect reviewer, cross-agent design decisions are compile-checked against a shared doc store with automatic reconciliation, and measurement runs continuously (offline + online + trace-clustering) rather than as a one-time launch gate.
The out-of-the-box default every session starts from unless changed: Manual permission mode, prompting for approval on first use of each tool -- maximum supervision, one approval at a time.

First deliberate loosening of supervision: acceptEdits mode automatically approves file edits and common filesystem commands in the working directory while still gating everything else -- a narrow, mechanical delegation rather than a general trust decision.

Suppresses the agent's clarifying questions rather than approving a narrow category of actions: the agent makes its own judgment calls instead of asking for input, a step beyond acceptEdits-style auto-approval, but still bounded to one step at a time -- it doesn't yet continue working through successive steps unattended the way full autonomous mode does.

Uses a deliberate baseline constraint -- committing to zero manually-written code for a defined scope of work -- as a forcing function that makes the team build the tooling/environment the agent actually needs, rather than falling back to hand-writing under time pressure. Explicitly not a permanent end state.

Deliberately loosens process friction (blocking-merge norms, waiting on flaky-test reruns) specifically because agent throughput makes corrections cheap relative to waiting -- an explicit, conditional tradeoff tied to actually having high throughput, not a universal default.

Removes manual context-transcription between where an issue is reported and where the agent acts on it -- e.g. wiring a bug-report channel directly into the agent's tool access -- instead of a human relaying the report by hand.

Autonomy extends across sessions and tasks with explicit backpressure: relaxed permission gating is paired with a self-verification mechanism rather than either full blocking or full unsupervision, multi-session work splits into specialized roles that hand off cleanly via logged state, and the agent gets the same direct access to the running system (CLI, browser, logs, observability) a human would use rather than only human-mediated summaries.

Agents run genuinely unattended against real correctness backpressure (compiler/type-system/test gates, not human review) as the actual gate; deployment itself accounts for agents being mid-task at any point (gradual traffic-shifting instead of a hard cutover); and the improvement loop -- diagnose, fix, measure, recommend ship/iterate/drop -- is fully agent-run, past merely agent-assisted.

Runs exactly one session at a time, start to finish, before starting the next -- parallel execution isn't part of the workflow at all, deliberately or otherwise. Weakest grounding in this ladder: no source states this baseline directly, inferred (like the other rung-1 floors below) from what a doc describing several parallel approaches implicitly presupposes as the case before any is adopted.

The mechanical precondition for real parallel work, not yet a scaled practice: running the same session in two terminals without an isolation mechanism doesn't act independently -- messages from both interleave into one shared transcript -- so adopting git worktrees (or an equivalent per-session isolation) is what actually makes concurrent sessions possible, before any of the tab/pane-based scaling above it.

First coordination primitive beyond mere file isolation: sessions can pass findings and status directly to each other (cross-session messaging) even without a structured division of labor yet -- the raw capability precedes any designed multi-session workflow built on top of it.

Runs a second session deliberately for quality rather than throughput: a Writer/Reviewer pattern where one session implements and a second, in fresh context and therefore unbiased toward code it just wrote, reviews the diff and reports issues back -- purpose-built for review, an earlier stage than the general-purpose numeric-scaling delegation above it.

Runs several sessions concurrently in an opportunistic, ad hoc burst -- kicking off a new agent for each new idea as it comes up during a brainstorm, then coming back later to review what each produced -- without yet having a governing rule for how many to run or when. Explicitly leaving scope to feel, distinct from rung 6's deliberate numeric-scaling discipline.

Runs multiple agent sessions concurrently at individual scale (terminal tabs or tmux panes, or racing two independent implementation plans and keeping whichever lands), relies on notifications rather than active polling to know which session needs attention, and gives delegation explicit numeric scaling rules (how many subagents for how complex a task) rather than leaving scope to feel.

Scales beyond a single machine or session (cloud-hosted sessions run 5-10 at once, fully isolated managed environments per coordinator-delegated piece) and starts running parallel at two levels simultaneously -- subagents concurrent with each other AND each subagent's own tool calls concurrent -- while treating the resulting human cognitive/context-switching load as a real, rising cost to manage rather than a side effect to ignore.

Scales to dozens or hundreds of concurrent agents via structural role-splitting (cheap worker models execute, expensive planner models only plan, keeping each agent's context narrow) and automated safety-classifier gating instead of manual per-action approval, accepting a real cost premium as the price of throughput -- and treats the human's own attention as the bottleneck resource to engineer for (a status dashboard) rather than agent throughput.
Model choice is inherited: a session simply runs on whatever model is configured as the default and /model is never invoked -- no routing decision has actually been made, deliberate or otherwise.

First deliberate routing act, but still ad hoc: manually switch models mid-session with /model when a task feels like it needs a different one, without weighing that the switch discards the session's prompt cache and forces the whole conversation to reprocess uncached.

Matches model choice to task type by hand, following documented guidance rather than switching on a whim: a fast/cheap model for quick edits and simple questions, a stronger reasoning model for architecture-level or multi-file debugging, a different tier again for pure completions -- deliberate and task-differentiated, but still a manual, per-call decision, not yet a fixed personal policy or a system making the call.

Delegates the routing decision itself to an automatic system rather than making the call by hand each time or committing to a fixed personal rule: a router combines real-time system health/availability with task-complexity evaluation to pick the model, matching straightforward tasks to faster/cheaper models and reserving costlier reasoning models for what actually needs them -- one less decision made, but not yet a strategy the practitioner authored themselves.

Routing is either deliberately simple (default to the largest/most capable model for everything, on the reasoning that needing less steering beats being slower per-call) or handed to policy (an admin-defined per-workspace model allowlist, with automatic per-task routing choosing only within it) rather than picked ad hoc per call.

Model choice becomes an explicitly documented, re-evaluated decision -- a living, dated changelog naming exactly which model handles which task type and why -- with independent-model consensus used for high-stakes calls instead of trusting one model's output alone.

Routing becomes a learned, production-informed system -- a complexity predictor plus a task-taxonomy router trained on real traffic, not benchmarks -- paired with the recognition that a model upgrade is not guaranteed to be a strict improvement for an existing harness, and can regress a specific workflow even while improving generally.

Routing logic lives in the harness itself, not an API gateway in front of it, because only the harness holds the task state (cache warmth, stalled progress, remaining work) needed to judge a switch before assembling model-specific tool definitions -- and a mid-session model switch is treated as a real, quantified cost decision (cache-miss reprocessing can run 5-10x) rather than a free choice.

Zero deliberate context management: let the built-in automatic compaction handle a full window whenever it happens, and take no action before or around it -- a full context window doesn't end the session by default, with or without any practice at all.

First deliberate act, still reactive rather than structured: manually clear the conversation when switching to unrelated work, because old conversation crowds out what's needed next and costs tokens on every message -- a one-off habit, not yet the target-utilization discipline of higher rungs.

Configures a persistent way to see context usage as it grows -- a status line showing a color-coded usage percentage and token counts, refreshed continuously -- turning context management from something noticed only once it becomes a problem into something visible by default.

Runs /compact deliberately at a chosen moment -- when context is visibly starting to affect response quality, or proactively before starting a long new task -- rather than waiting for automatic compaction or reactively clearing on a topic switch. Preserves a structured summary of what came before instead of discarding it outright.

Begins actively protecting the primary context window: expensive exploratory work (search, grep, log-reading, test-run summarizing) gets isolated into a disposable subagent window instead of filling the main one, and progress gets written to persistent notes outside the window (a to-do list, a NOTES.md) so it survives context resets.

Context management becomes a structured, repo-level discipline: the whole workflow, not just single sessions, is organized around keeping window utilization in a target range via a research-then-plan-then-implement cycle; memory is deliberately externalized (CLAUDE.md, per-task notes directories) and continuously edited as corrections happen; sessions can be forked to explore a risky branch without losing the original; and any workflow repeated more than once a day gets promoted into a reusable skill or slash command.

Memory and context infrastructure become team-owned and mechanically maintained rather than individually curated: a shared instruction file is edited by the whole team multiple times a week as a living document; a background agent scans for documentation staleness against actual code and opens its own fix-up PRs; and subagents write large structured outputs directly to a filesystem or external store, passing back only a lightweight reference instead of copying everything through the lead agent's context.

The top-level instruction file shrinks to a short map or table-of-contents (~100 lines) pointing into a real docs/ directory that is the actual system of record, and agents themselves become responsible for curating a shared knowledge folder under a hard line-budget constraint -- capturing precisely the surprising, non-obvious things a new agent would otherwise have to rediscover the hard way.
